name: VIP (Vasoactive intestinal peptide)
lead: Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) is a 28-amino-acid neuropeptide found in the gut, brain, heart, lungs and other tissues. It acts through the VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors and has vasodilating, smooth-muscle-relaxing and immune-modulating effects.[1][2] In peptide and recovery communities it is listed among research peptides, where vendors link its vasodilating and anti-inflammatory biology to recovery, circulation and tissue health, which people connect with training capacity and overall appearance.

VIP is sold online in some peptide markets as a research compound. Published human research on injected VIP itself is limited to small physiological and headache-provocation studies, a Phase 1 study in respiratory distress and sepsis, and a registered COPD study, alongside larger trials of its synthetic form aviptadil in COVID-19.[3][4][5][7][9] No study of VIP for appearance was found.

Beyond its physiology, VIP has a clinical history through aviptadil, which was approved in the UK in 2000 in combination with phentolamine for erectile dysfunction and was later developed for COVID-19 respiratory failure.[8]

paras: VIP relaxes smooth muscle in the gut, gallbladder and airways, stimulates water and electrolyte secretion in the intestine, and causes coronary and peripheral vasodilation. In the brain, it is an important synchroniser of circadian rhythm in the suprachiasmatic nucleus.[1] A review of its cardiovascular effects notes that it is 50 to 100 times more potent than acetylcholine as a vasodilator on a molar basis.[6]

Clinically, VIP is overproduced in VIPomas, and VIP signalling is altered in inflammatory bowel disease.[1] Its short half-life of about two minutes in blood is one reason analogues such as aviptadil exist.[1]

VIP also relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter and stomach, boosts pancreatic bicarbonate, lowers arterial blood pressure and has positive inotropic and chronotropic effects on the heart, according to Wikipedia.[1] In the brain it acts as a key synchroniser of the suprachiasmatic nucleus, the body's master circadian pacemaker: binding of VPAC2 raises cyclic AMP, activates protein kinase A and CREB and can drive Per1 and Per2 expression in the circadian clock.[1] The article also notes VIP involvement in mast-cell communication in inflammatory bowel disease and research interest in heart failure.[1]

VIP binds two class II G protein-coupled receptors, VPAC1 and VPAC2. Activation of VPAC2 triggers a G-alpha cascade that raises cyclic AMP and activates protein kinase A, which phosphorylates the transcription factor CREB; this can drive Per1 and Per2 expression and so influence the molecular circadian clock [1]. VIP is frequently co-released with GABA, which shapes neuronal firing patterns [1].

In the intestine VIP also suppresses gastric acid secretion and stimulates pepsinogen release, and in the airways it relaxes tracheal smooth muscle [1]. These vasodilating and smooth-muscle-relaxing effects are the basis for the interest in VIP and its analogue aviptadil in lung inflammation, asthma and COPD [8].

sections.h: How it is connected to appearance and recovery
paras: VIP is not an approved cosmetic or sports ingredient, and Wikipedia describes no skin or hair function for it [1]. The link made in peptide and recovery communities runs through its biology: a potent vasodilator and immune-modulating signal that vendors associate with circulation, inflammation control and recovery, which proponents connect with training capacity and physique [1][6]. People discussing the peptide online typically treat it alongside other research peptides rather than as a stand-alone appearance compound.

VIP is a member of the glucagon and secretin peptide superfamily and a ligand of class II G protein-coupled receptors; it is also known as vasoactive intestinal polypeptide.[1] The human gene, VIP, is on chromosome 6 at band 6q25.2 and the mouse ortholog is on chromosome 10.[1] Wikipedia gives its half-life in blood as about two minutes.[1]

Aviptadil is a synthetic form of human VIP. Wikipedia states that VIP was first characterised in 1970, that aviptadil combined with phentolamine (Invicorp) was approved in the UK in October 2000 as an intracavernosal treatment for erectile dysfunction, that the FDA granted it fast-track designation for COVID-19 respiratory distress in June 2020, and that India approved it as Oxyptadil in April 2022 for severe COVID-19 with ARDS.[8]

The ACTIV-3b/TESICO randomised trial enrolled 473 participants at 28 US sites in a 2x2 factorial design with remdesivir; the aviptadil comparison included 231 aviptadil and 230 placebo participants, and the data and safety monitoring board recommended stopping the aviptadil trial for futility on 25 May 2022.[9] A 2025 systematic review of nine studies (two randomised trials and seven case series, 665 patients) found a pooled survival odds ratio of 1.01 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.42), and a 2025 randomised trial of inhaled aviptadil in 80 hospitalised adults reported shorter time to discharge (7.8 versus 10 days).[10][11]

According to Wikipedia, VIP is produced in the heart, where it causes coronary vasodilation and positive inotropic and chronotropic effects, and it also dilates peripheral vessels and lowers arterial blood pressure.[1] In the gut it relaxes the lower oesophageal sphincter, stomach and gallbladder and stimulates water and electrolyte secretion into pancreatic juice and bile.[1] It is also found in a subtype of inhibitory cortical interneuron, and VIP neurons in the hypothalamus influence prolactin and, in some vertebrates, social behaviour such as parental care and aggression.[1]

Wikipedia lists research interest in heart failure, in osteoarthritis (where evidence conflicts on whether VIP is up- or down-regulated, although VIP has protected cartilage in animal studies) and in inflammatory bowel disease, where mast-cell VIP signalling is upregulated in colitis and Crohn's disease.[1] A small clinical study of tear VIP after laser keratorefractive surgery looked at dry eye, a separate context.[13]

Wikipedia's aviptadil article says the US-Israeli company NeuroRx partnered with Relief Therapeutics to develop it in the United States under names including RLF-100 and Zyesami, that NeuroRx requested an emergency use authorization for critically ill COVID-19 patients in September 2020, and that Zuventus Healthcare sought and received approval in India, where it was granted marketing permission as Oxyptadil in April 2022. The article carries a promotional-tone warning and says that its efficacy statements lack citations.[8]

Small trials have given intravenous VIP to study its effects rather than to treat appearance concerns. In migraine research, infusions in migraine patients and healthy volunteers were used to examine headache and cranial blood-flow responses.[3][4] An early Phase 1 study examined VIP in acute respiratory distress syndrome and sepsis,[5] and a registered study examined VIP in COPD with pulmonary hypertension.[7]
The synthetic analogue aviptadil has been tested in COVID-19 respiratory failure; see the Aviptadil article. No studies of VIP in cosmetic, recovery or performance contexts were found.

In the TESICO trial of intravenous aviptadil in COVID-19 respiratory failure, a safety board recommended stopping for futility.[9] The Lancet Respiratory Medicine published a comment on that trial under the title "A negative trial for vasoactive intestinal peptide in COVID-19-associated acute hypoxaemic respiratory failure".[12]

VIP is listed by some online vendors as a research compound, with claims about immune and inflammatory regulation and circulation. These claims come from marketing and community discussion; no human trial has tested VIP for the uses advertised, and the human research that exists uses clinical or provocation settings rather than recovery or appearance.

VIP is listed by some online vendors as a research compound, with claims about immune and inflammatory regulation and circulation; these claims come from marketing and community discussion rather than from trials.[1] In these communities it sits alongside other research peptides used in the pursuit of recovery and physical improvement. Aviptadil, the synthetic form, is a regulated medicine in the countries where it is approved, and VIP itself has no approved therapeutic use according to Wikipedia.[1][8]

timeline.event: Phase 1 study of VIP in ARDS and sepsis begins.[5]
Aviptadil with phentolamine approved in the UK for erectile dysfunction.[8]
FDA fast-track designation for aviptadil in COVID-19 respiratory distress.[8]
Expanded-access and phase 3 ACTIV-3b/TESICO trials of intravenous aviptadil begin; NRx reports positive results in May and files for emergency use authorization [8][9].
TESICO safety board recommends stopping the aviptadil trial for futility on 25 May; India approves Oxyptadil in April.[8][9]
Systematic review of aviptadil in ARDS reports a pooled survival odds ratio near 1.0, and a randomised trial of inhaled aviptadil in 80 adults reports shorter time to discharge.[10][11]

lore.intro: VIP appears in peptide and recovery communities as one of many research peptides, with claims about circulation, inflammation and recovery drawn largely from its physiology and vendor listings.

claims.believers: Proponents point to VIP being a potent vasodilator, reported as 50 to 100 times more potent than acetylcholine on a molar basis, and expect better blood flow to aid recovery [6].
claims.experts: Human work on infused VIP is physiological and headache-provocation research, and its half-life in blood is about two minutes; no study tests it for recovery or appearance [1][3][4].

claims.claim: VIP calms inflammation and regulates the immune system
claims.believers: Vendors and users cite VIP's immune-modulating signalling, including mast-cell communication in the gut [1].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes VIP involvement in inflammatory bowel disease signalling; clinical trials of its synthetic form aviptadil in ARDS and COVID-19 did not show a clear survival benefit in pooled analysis [1][10].

claims.claim: Aviptadil showed that VIP therapy helps severe COVID-19
claims.believers: Developers reported positive results in 2021 and India approved Oxyptadil in April 2022 for severe COVID-19 with ARDS [8].
claims.experts: The TESICO safety board recommended stopping the aviptadil trial for futility in May 2022, and a 2025 meta-analysis reported a pooled survival odds ratio of 1.01; a 2025 inhaled-aviptadil trial reported shorter time to discharge [9][10][11].

claims.claim: VIP regulates sleep and body clock
claims.believers: Circadian-interest communities cite VIP's role in the suprachiasmatic nucleus [1].
claims.experts: VIP is documented as a key synchroniser of the body's master circadian pacemaker, acting through VPAC2, cAMP and Per gene expression [1].

claims.claim: Injected or nasal VIP is a safe recovery peptide
claims.believers: Vendors list it among research compounds for recovery and circulation.
claims.experts: Infusions in migraine studies provoked headache and vascular effects, and no safety data exist for the research-peptide use pattern [3][4].

chain: VIP relaxes smooth muscle and dilates blood vessels
Vendors link this and its immune-modulating biology to circulation and recovery
Better recovery and training capacity, which people connect with physique and overall appearance
angle.text: VIP is a natural vasodilating, anti-inflammatory-signalling neuropeptide that some peptide vendors list among recovery compounds. The link to appearance runs through circulation, recovery and training capacity; no human study has tested VIP for those outcomes.

card.summary: A natural vasodilating neuropeptide sold as a research peptide, with human appearance use not yet studied.
card.note: Human studies are small physiology or headache-provocation trials; not studied for appearance.

quick.overview:
VIP is a natural 28-amino-acid peptide that widens blood vessels, relaxes smooth muscle and modulates immune activity. Some vendors list it as a research peptide.

Human trials of VIP are small and aimed at physiology, headache or lung disease. None tests it for appearance or recovery.
quick.mechanism: It binds VPAC1 and VPAC2 receptors, raising cyclic AMP in target cells. Its half-life in blood is about two minutes.
quick.risks: Intravenous VIP was used in migraine studies to provoke headache, showing it can have vascular effects. No safety data exist for the research-peptide use pattern.
